structured_output.ground: "Praise belongs to God, Lord of the worlds." The sentence is nominal and has no verb. It states as a standing fact that praise, all of it or the praise that is due, belongs to God. God is then described as the rabb, the master and nurturer, of the ʿālamīn: all the kinds of created beings. Nobody is named as the one who praises. The speaker "we" appears only at 1:5.

triggers.how: B001 and B002 of the same root read together. The full entries say 'balawtuhu fa-aḥmadtuhu': I tested him and found him praiseworthy. They also give 'aḥmadtu al-arḍ': I found the land good to live in or graze.
The worlds are ʿālam, things that make known (ع ل م B003). They supply the evidence on which a verdict of praise can rest.

findings.statement: Praise belongs to God. It is also the kind of praise that comes as a verdict: the praiser has tried something, lived in it, and found it good.
findings.perceptible: Ḥamd is heard as a finding reached after experience, not as flattery or a reflex formula. The praise has a history: someone has lived under this Lord and in these worlds and judged them good. The unspoken praiser has already tested before speaking.

triggers.how: Shared scene trade.gift. Niʿma, the favour, is named only at the end of the surah.
ر ب ب B016: rubā, favour and kindness (minor).
ه د ي hadiyya, the gift gently sent (plan I7).

findings.statement: Praise belongs to God as praise and also as thanks for a favour (B001: shukr ʿalā al-niʿma). The favour itself is not named until 'those You have favoured' at 1:7.
findings.perceptible: The surah gives thanks before it says what it is thanking for. Its opening word answers a gift the surah names only at its last turn (anʿamta). The whole surah is framed as a thanks and its occasion.

triggers.how: ر ب ب B007: marabb al-ibil, the place where the camels stay. B014: rabrab, the herd.
The ḍālla is the beast in the waste whose rabb is not known (plan I2).
Wasm, the brand, opened I2 at 1:1.

findings.statement: Praise belongs to God. Beside the plain sense, it also carries the herder's word for land found good to graze and dwell in (aḥmadtu al-arḍ), spoken about the rabb whose name also means the camels' resting-place.
findings.perceptible: Praise can be heard as the settled contentment of animals that have found their pasture and fold good. The stray at 1:7, far from its fold and unknown to any owner, has no such ground to praise.

triggers.how: The first person 'we' appears only at 1:5.
The nominative, nominal sentence. The Tahdhib reports a Bedouin variant with the accusative (al-ḥamda), which implies the verb 'I praise'.

findings.statement: The praise is stated as a fact that simply holds, with no verb, tense or speaker. It holds whoever says it, and it is still true before anyone says it.
findings.perceptible: The sentence does not say 'I praise' or 'let us praise'. It reports that praise already stands in God's possession. The reciter steps into a praise that is already there, and becomes a 'we' only at 1:5, when they turn to face God.

triggers.how: The definite article al- together with the preposition li-.

findings.statement: The al- of al-ḥamd can be heard as 'all praise' or as 'the praise that is due'. The li- marks belonging and entitlement: praise is God's property, not only something addressed to Him.
findings.perceptible: The same possessive li- will be answered by rabb (owner) and mālik (possessor, 1:4). The verse is built from the language of ownership: praise belongs to God, and God owns the worlds.

triggers.how: The concordance lists the full phrase al-ḥamdu li-llāhi rabbi l-ʿālamīn. It closes 6:45 (after the wrongdoers are cut off), 10:10 (the last word of the people of the Garden), 37:182 (the end of the surah) and 39:75 (after judgment is passed).

findings.statement: 'Praise belongs to God, Lord of the worlds' is elsewhere the closing word spoken when things are settled. Here the same words open the recitation.
findings.perceptible: The Fātiḥa begins with the words that end history, the judgment and life in the Garden. Heard this way, the reciter starts with the conclusion before walking the road toward it (1:4 the Day, 1:6 the road).

triggers.how: The form ḥamādāk: 'your utmost', the praiseworthy end one can reach.
A road, and so an end to reach (travel.route).

findings.statement: Praise belongs to God. The root also knows ḥamādāk, 'the utmost worth reaching', so the verse can be heard as naming praise's furthest end.
findings.perceptible: Praise has a direction and an end point, a goal to be reached. This anticipates the road of 1:6.

triggers.how: The rabb is the one who provides and brings to completion (B002, B016). Providing is what earns thanks.
The favour is given.

findings.statement: Praise belongs to God. The root also knows taḥammud, laying claim to praise by reminding people of one's gifts, and against that background the praise here is owed to the one giver whose claim to thanks is rightful rather than a boast.
findings.perceptible: Among people, demanding praise for your giving is blameworthy ('he who spends on himself may not taḥammad over people'). Here the praise is assigned outright to the giver. That shows the giving was to others, not to himself.

triggers.how: The collective 'we'.

findings.statement: Praise belongs to God. The idiom aḥmadu ilayka Allāh, 'I praise God together with you', lies behind praise spoken with no named speaker.
findings.perceptible: The unnamed praise can be shared: praising God together with a companion. This prepares for the plural 'we' at 1:5.

triggers.how: rule.ownership and rule.kingship: possessor and king.
Dominion and obedience.
The ʿabd, the one owned.

findings.statement: God is Lord of the worlds in the sense in which Arabic says rabb al-dār (owner of the house) and rabb al-dābba (owner of the beast). The worlds are His household and His herd.
findings.perceptible: Rabb is an everyday word of ownership and mastery, not only a divine title. This opens the household of I4: owner here, king at 1:4, the owned one speaking at 1:5.

triggers.how: Raḥim, the womb (I3, opened at 1:1).
Repeated right after rabb al-ʿālamīn, so the rabb is wrapped in womb-words on both sides.
B005 rābba/rabīb: foster-mother and foster-child. B009: the ewe that has just given birth.

findings.statement: God is Lord of the worlds as the one who raises them: repairs, tends and completes each thing stage by stage (tarbiya ḥālan fa-ḥālan).
findings.perceptible: Lordship becomes a process in time: a child raised, a crop brought to ripeness. Placed between raḥmān raḥīm at 1:1 and 1:3, the rabb reads as a nurturer surrounded by womb-mercy.

triggers.how: B001 owner, B002 raising and completing, B007 staying and lasting, B008 the cloud that hangs and nourishes plants, B013 gathered abundant water, B012 the evergreen plant. These are branches of one root.

findings.statement: Rabb is the one who owns something and also the one who stays by it and brings it to completion. Its branches share one concept: remaining with a thing and making it whole.
findings.perceptible: Across the branches, rabb names a presence that lasts: a cloud that stays over the ground, a camel-fold one returns to, water that collects, a plant that stays green, an owner who does not leave his property but tends it. Owning and nurturing turn out to be one act.

triggers.how: Wasm, the brand (I2).
The hādī, the lead animal.
The ḍālla, the stray whose rabb is not known.
B014 rabrab: the herd.

findings.statement: God is Lord of the worlds. Among its senses, rabb holds the owner of the herd and the marabb, the place where the camels stay and to which they return.
findings.perceptible: The dictionary defines the stray of 1:7 as the beast 'whose rabb is not known'. The word used for God here is the word the surah's last danger is defined against. Belonging to this rabb is the opposite of straying.

triggers.how: B001 knowing, B002 mark/banner/waymark, B003 the world as a sign pointing to its maker ('because it is a mark in itself and points').

findings.statement: The ʿālamīn are all created kinds. The root that names them names things that make something known: knowledge, the mark, the banner, the waymark. So each world is also a sign of its maker.
findings.perceptible: The Turkish reader hears âlem, ilim and alâmet as three separate words. In Arabic they are one root. 'Lord of the worlds' is also 'Lord of everything that makes Him known'. The universe is a field of signs that point beyond themselves, and that is the ground on which praise can be a verdict (F1).

triggers.how: travel.route: the guide and the direction.
travel.route: the road.
travel.route: the one who strays.

findings.statement: God is Lord of the worlds. The worlds can also be heard as maʿālim al-ṭarīq, the waymarks set along a road.
findings.perceptible: Before the reciter asks for the road (1:6), the surah has already called all created things marks. The road of 1:6 runs through a landscape posted with waymarks, and straying is failing to read them.

triggers.how: Shared scene sign.marking: ism heard through wasm/sima, the brand.
The owner of the beast (B001).

findings.statement: God is Lord of the worlds. The ʿālamīn are also the marked things (ʿalam, ʿalāma), each carrying a sign of whose it is.
findings.perceptible: Together with bismi at 1:1 (the brand), the worlds become the owner's marked herd. The universe carries God's mark the way a camel carries the brand of its rabb, which gives the stray of 1:7 its full weight.

triggers.how: The concordance: 42 of 73 uses are in the phrase rabb al-ʿālamīn. Another 14 uses name a population of peoples, as in 2:47, 'I favoured you over the ʿālamīn'.

findings.statement: In the Quran ʿālamīn is mostly bound to rabb. Elsewhere it often means 'the peoples' or 'all people'. The 'worlds' include, and often mean, living communities.
findings.perceptible: 'Worlds' can sound like cosmic spheres or planets. In Quranic use the word is closer to 'all the kinds of beings, peoples above all'. The rabb is master of populations that can know Him.

triggers.how: -īn, the sound masculine plural ending, which is usually reserved for beings that know.

findings.statement: ʿĀlamīn pluralises a word (ʿālam) that already names a whole kind. The -īn ending is normally used for rational beings, so it is a plural of kinds framed as knowers.
findings.perceptible: The form treats every class of creatures as if it were a group of knowers. This matches the root sense of 'that which knows and makes known'.

triggers.how: ritual.prayer and divine.lordship: worship.
worship/obedience.

findings.statement: Praise belongs to God. Within God's name the root keeps ilāh, 'the one made the object of worship' (alaha, taʾallaha = to worship).
findings.perceptible: The name already contains the service that 1:5 will declare. The Turkish reader keeps Allah (the proper name) and ilah (any god) apart and so misses that link.

triggers.how: emotion.love and kin.birth_nursing (womb).
B005 rābba, the foster-mother (kin.birth_nursing).
Bewilderment and loss.

findings.statement: Praise belongs to God. In a documented alternative derivation of the name from و ل ه, God is the one toward whom creatures turn in walah: bewildered longing, like a mother's for a lost child.
findings.perceptible: The name can carry longing and bewilderment, which fits the womb (raḥim) and foster-mother (rābba) words around it. The rabb who raises is also the one missed when absent.

triggers.how: B005 foster child (kin.birth_nursing).
The same alternative root in the basmala.

findings.statement: Under the alternative derivation, the name echoes tawlīh, separating a mother from her child until she is wāliha. The praise is addressed to the one whose absence would be that separation.
findings.perceptible: This is a faint undertone that deepens I3 (the womb and the raiser). It is kept on record only.

triggers.how: water.rain_cloud: cloud and rain in the same scene.
B012, the plant that stays green. B013, gathered abundant water. B002, growth.

findings.statement: God is Lord of the worlds. Rabb also holds the rabāb, the layered cloud said to be named for raising plants or for lasting.
findings.perceptible: This gives a material picture of lordship: a cloud that lingers over the land and makes things grow and stay green. It is the nurturing of F11 as weather.

triggers.how: war.protection: the ally.
war.protection: the protected client.
rule.covenant: witness.

findings.statement: God is Lord of the worlds. Rabb's family also holds rabāba, the pact of protection and neighbourhood.
findings.perceptible: Lordship includes a bond of protection. The help asked for at 1:5 can be heard as a claim made under a pact rather than an unsecured plea.

triggers.how: A plural of kinds or peoples.
B010, the rabāba bag that holds all the arrows. B014, the herd.

findings.statement: God is Lord of the worlds. Rabb's family also names gathered multitudes (ribba, ribbiyyūn, the tribes of al-Ribāb) and the case that holds all the arrows together.
findings.perceptible: The word for the Lord also names the gathering itself. The ʿālamīn are held together as one assembled company.

triggers.how: Mercy follows immediately.
Owner/king of the Day.
The owned ones speak.

findings.statement: God's lordship over the worlds is stated in the third person. Mercy follows at once (1:3), then kingship over the Day (1:4), and only then is He addressed as 'You' (1:5).
findings.perceptible: Rabb stands at the head of a sequence of mastery: owner, then merciful, then king of the reckoning, then the one faced directly. Ownership is softened by mercy before it becomes judgment.

triggers.how: trade.gift: favour.
B016 rubā: need, favour, and the tight knot.

findings.statement: God is Lord of the worlds. The rare rubā, meaning both need and favour, lets the rabb be heard as the one who meets need with favour.
findings.perceptible: A minor member of I7. The need of the worlds and the favour given to them sit in one word-family.

triggers.how: Tahdhib: al-Farrāʾ says the Qurʾān readers agree on the nominative. Some desert Arabs said al-ḥamda (accusative, 'I praise the praise'), al-ḥamdi lillāhi, or al-ḥamdu lullāhi.

findings.statement: The recited text keeps the nominative, which states praise as fact. The reported non-canonical accusative would imply a verb and a speaker, 'I praise'.
findings.perceptible: The contrast makes F4 audible. The chosen form has no one performing the praise; praise simply holds.

triggers.how: A non-canonical reading rabba al-ʿālamīn in the accusative (praise or address) is recalled; it is not in the variants given.

findings.statement: God is Lord of the worlds. A recalled reading in the accusative would set rabb apart as an exclamation of praise, or as address ('O Lord…'), leaning toward 1:5.
findings.perceptible: It would anticipate the turn to direct address, but it rests on memory only.

triggers.how: water.well: B013, gathered abundant water.

findings.statement: God is Lord of the worlds. The ع ل م root also names the ʿaylam, the deep well full of water.
findings.perceptible: This is a faint material echo of depth and abundance beside rabb's gathered water. It is kept on record only.

loaded_words.role: The fixed attribution al-ḥamdu li-llāh / lahu al-ḥamd, often as a closing word when something is settled (6:45, 10:10, 37:182, 39:75)
loaded_words.count: 28 of 43 (14 more with a tasbīḥ verb, bi-ḥamdi)
loaded_words.departure: Here it opens rather than closes. Turkish 'hamd' / 'hamdolsun' is heard as thanks or relief after something goes well. The Arabic role is a declaration that praise is God's.

loaded_words.role: Complement of rabb in rabb al-ʿālamīn. Secondarily it names the population of peoples
loaded_words.count: 42 of 73 with rabb; 14 as a comparison population of peoples
loaded_words.departure: 'Worlds' / 'âlemler' suggests cosmic spheres. Quranic use leans to all kinds of beings, peoples above all.

loaded_words.role: No single dominant role. Addressed in petitions, source in genitives, subject, object of worship
loaded_words.departure: Translations fix it as the title 'Lord' / 'Rab'. The everyday senses of owner, master and raiser are lost.

loaded_words.role: Mostly the clause subject or topic
loaded_words.departure: Here it is not the subject but the possessor after li-: praise belongs to Him.

losses.loses: Praise for qualities and deeds, and praise as a verdict reached after testing something (aḥmadtuhu: I found him good). It also loses the sense of a standing fact: the Arabic has no verb or wish.
losses.adds: 'Hamdolsun' is optative ('let praise be') and is used as a sigh of relief after escaping trouble. That narrows ḥamd to thanks for luck.

losses.loses: The reader does not hear that these familiar names are ḥamd forms: 'the most praised', 'the much-praised', 'the praised'.
losses.adds: They sound like ordinary personal names.

losses.loses: The plain possessive and entitlement of li-: praise is God's own, the same ownership language as rabb and mālik.
losses.adds: 'Mahsus' (reserved exclusively for) adds a note of exclusivity. It is a common Turkish rendering.

losses.loses: The owner of a house or a beast, the master who is obeyed, the one who stays by a thing and raises it stage by stage.
losses.adds: A near-proper name for God, cut off from everyday ownership.

losses.loses: Tending, repairing and bringing to completion step by step. The same root is in Rab, but the reader cannot hear it.
losses.adds: Schooling, manners and discipline, even punishment ('terbiye etmek' = to teach someone a lesson).

losses.loses: The link to ilim (knowledge) and alâmet (sign), and to waymarks and banners. The worlds are marks that point to their maker. It also loses the Quranic lean toward 'peoples'.
losses.adds: Cosmic realms or spheres. In colloquial Turkish 'âlem' also means a scene, a crowd, or a party ('âlem yapmak').

grammar: The sentence is nominal, with no verb or speaker: praise is stated as a standing fact, not as the act 'I praise'. The 'we' appears only at 1:5.
al-ḥamd: the article can mean 'all praise' (the whole genus) or 'the praise that is due'. Turkish 'hamd' without an article hides this.
li-llāh: the li- of belonging and entitlement. It is the same ownership grammar that rabb (owner) and mālik (1:4) continue.
rabbi is genitive because it describes Allāh (in apposition to Him). It is not a new sentence, so 'Lord of the worlds' says who the owner of praise is.
ʿālamīn: a sound masculine plural in -īn, normally used for rational beings, applied to a word that already means a whole kind. It is a plural of kinds framed as knowers.
variants: The Tahdhib (al-Farrāʾ) reports that Qurʾān readers agree on the nominative al-ḥamdu. Bedouin usage had al-ḥamda (accusative, which implies 'I praise'), al-ḥamdi lillāhi and al-ḥamdu lullāhi. The contrast highlights that the canonical form states praise as a fact without a speaker.
A recalled non-canonical rabba al-ʿālamīn (accusative, as praise or address) would lean toward the direct address of 1:5. It is not in the variants given (memory).
structured_output.reread: Praise already belongs to God before anyone says it, and the sentence names no praiser. It is the praise of someone who has lived in the worlds, tested them, and found their owner good, the way a herder finds a pasture good to settle in. The one praised is the rabb: the owner of the house and the herd, and also the one who stays by what he owns and raises it stage by stage to completion, like a lingering cloud over growing land. What he owns are the ʿālamīn. They are all the kinds of beings, and in the same root they are marks, signs and waymarks that make their maker known and carry his brand. So the verse is at once thanks for a favour the surah will name only at its end, a verdict drawn from the signs, and a statement of belonging. The stray at 1:7, 'whose rabb is not known', is defined against it.

set_aside.why: It is a function word that shares only letters with rabb. It has no semantic link to the ayah.

set_aside.why: Its 'iṣlāḥ bihi' (repairing with it) echoes B002, but the material image (coating skins, sweet dishes) completes nothing in the surah. It is folded into the repair and completion concept of F12 instead.

set_aside.why: They form a weak pairing with ʿālamīn B001 (knowing) and with naʿbudu as 'ship', but they belong to other lemmas and add nothing perceptible to 'Lord of the worlds' here.

set_aside.why: These are mechanical role matches with no dictionary branch of this ayah behind them. The blame side of the surah is carried by maghḍūb and ḍāllīn at 1:7, not by these words.

set_aside.what: The trade.sale and war.battle scenes built on و ل ه B002 (the mother separated from her child in sale or captivity)
set_aside.why: Only the separation and bewilderment facet is kept (F21, on record). The sale and battle frames around God's name add nothing that keeps the plain reading intact.
